v: This November, Calgary went under Stage four water restrictions. To understand why, follow one pipe.
The Bearspaw South Feeder Main. Built in nineteen seventy-five and about ten point eight kilometres long, it carries up to about sixty per cent of Calgary's drinking water.
On the evening of June fifth, twenty twenty-four, it failed. Robotic inspections then found five more spots at risk that needed emergency repairs.
In twenty twenty-four, the City repaired the break and twenty-nine more pipe segments, including those five, for about thirty-eight point two million dollars.
Then an independent review panel found something bigger. The risks behind the failure had been identified twenty years earlier, after another feeder main, McKnight, failed in two thousand four.

This pipe was designated for inspection in twenty seventeen, twenty twenty and twenty twenty-two. No inspections occurred. Requests to shut it down for inspection were repeatedly redirected or delayed.
On December thirtieth, twenty twenty-five, it broke again. About two more weeks of water restrictions and repairs followed.

The fix is a new steel pipe, the same size, running parallel to the old one. Crews tunnelled about three point seven kilometres, on a route that crosses sixteen Avenue, the Bow River and the CPKC rail line.
On November fourth, crews shut down the old main and began work to connect the new pipe. Stage four means no outdoor water use, for about four weeks.

The City expects the new pipe in service by the end of the year. Another section of the old main, on Parkdale Boulevard, needs proactive repairs at six locations, though the City says it is in good overall condition.
Twenty years from warning to failure. What other warnings are still waiting? Follow the evidence at calgary insight dot c a.
